cells.tense: You are in it now — the merge happened and you're still at the pen.
cells.ask: Set down one agreement for a day and see if the other person picks it back up without a reminder.
cells.core:
It's happening now, and you're the one holding it. Not just feeling close to someone — actually running two lives on one direction, because the connection was chosen and you chose well. This is when a merge stops being a maybe and becomes a current you're both standing in. What you built is landing in what comes next. You're not stuck at the finish. You're at the door, and the door opens because you finished something, not because you left something.

The carry is steady, but a merge still costs you something: when you've decided to flow together, you're spending your own direction on two. The move here isn't to guard it more. It's to let it move from feeling rather than from decision — keep the current fed by what you actually enjoy, not by what you've agreed to. What you protect next should come from that, not from duty.
cells.sheetLine: Two streams, one flow: you chose the join, and you keep it.
cells.verb: Chooses a genuine connection and lets two streams run as one flow
cells.place: Where what's been gathered is fully taken in and released into what comes next

cells.tense: You're already bracing for a merge that hasn't fully happened yet.
cells.ask: Do one joint thing at half the pace you'd normally push it, and let it finish on its own.
cells.core:
The merge is in your head before it's in the room. You're scanning for every place it could go wrong, tightening the plan to keep the two of you on one track — and the more you grip, the less space there is for the connection to do its own moving. You can't write the future from here. The picture you're protecting is real, but the way you're holding it is ahead of anything that's actually happened.

You don't have to lock the merge down for it to be good. What this needs is the opposite of forcing: growth that happens on its own once the conditions are right, care that doesn't exhaust itself, holding without clutching. Let one thing grow at its own speed this week instead of turning the pace up. The join holds better when you stop pulling it tighter.

cells.tense: There's a connection you can still remember landing, and why you stopped walking through that door isn't clear.
cells.ask: Say one small true thing to the other person before you're sure it's welcome.
cells.core:
A connection moved toward becoming one thing and didn't. Whatever it was, joining two lives didn't happen, and you've been standing on the near side ever since — not telling anyone it's still open. You don't need to decide why. You need one thing: to know your own read of what's true here without having to argue for it first. That knowing doesn't build something on top of nothing. It clears the air so you can see what's actually there.

The gap isn't in what you feel. You're waiting for certainty before you'll move, and you won't get it by staying back. One small true thing said or asked, before you're sure it will land, is the way the current comes back — and the door you thought was behind you is the one you're standing in.

cells.tense: You're already merging two lives in how you spend your days, and you're still calling it practical.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you do regularly because a connection matters to you, and stop calling it logistics.
cells.core:
The way you fit your days around someone, the small adjustments nobody asked for — that's a merge running quietly the whole time. You call it practical, or sensible, or just how things are. But the choice is being made, over and over, by you. It runs fine. What isn't happening is you saying so.

The connection isn't what's missing. The acknowledgment is. The same practice you're running right now is doing its work, but the way you talk about it makes it sound like it's not yours. That's what makes the care feel invisible after a while — not too little love, too little credit. Pick one thing you did today that was really about the two of you, and say that's what it was. The merge doesn't get stronger from that. It just stops being a thing you do without knowing why.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I'd flag: in the Too Little cell I located a room where the merge didn't land, which the record doesn't name; I moved it to 'you can remember it landing' — an invitation, not a claim about the past. A reader could reasonably say that a person in the Too Much state has had no merge start at all and my read of one already underway is wrong. The ask — lying down and letting someone's rhythm be the only one in the room — is still useful if I'm wrong, because it forces the habit to surface either way. The sentence that serves me more than the person: any version of 'you're already doing the merging' that makes my read sound deeper than their experience; if they say it's not happening, they should keep the practice anyway, and the cell says so.
